articles.title: Australia turns a former gold mine into a pumped-hydro storage hub, using two disused pits to store 2,000 MWh of electricity
articles.summary: Australia's Kidston Renewable Energy Hub is repurposing a former gold mine in Far North Queensland into a pumped-hydro energy storage facility.
articles.body: Australia's Kidston Renewable Energy Hub is repurposing a former gold mine in Far North Queensland into a pumped-hydro energy storage facility. The K2-Hydro project will use two disused mine pits as upper and lower reservoirs, with a planned capacity of 250 MW and 2,000 MWh of storage, providing approximately eight hours of energy storage. According to the Australian Renewable Energy Agency, the facility is designed to store electricity and release it when demand is high, with a start-up time expected to be less than 30 seconds. The project will also reuse existing mining infrastructure and connect the renewable energy hub to the national grid through a transmission line.How are former gold mine pits used for pumped-hydro storageThe K2-Hydro system is designed to use the former mine pits rather than constructing entirely new reservoirs. The project will effectively turn the existing pits into a large energy storage system. Water is pumped into an upper reservoir when electricity prices are low and is later released through reversible turbines into the lower reservoir to generate electricity when demand is high. The agency described the mine's massive open-cut pits as being repurposed to hold water for energy storage.According to The World Economic Forum, the project will source water from groundwater and rainfall. It also says the existing mining infrastructure, including cleared land and roads, is being reused as part of the development. The approach is intended to make use of infrastructure already present at the former mining site while combining the pumped-hydro facility with the solar installation. The stored energy can then be dispatched when required, including during peak demand or when cloudy conditions reduce solar generation.How much renewable energy can the pumped-hydro facility storeThe pumped-hydro facility has a planned capacity of 250 MW and 2,000 MWh of energy storage. ARENA states that this provides approximately eight hours of storage and would be enough to power 143,000 homes. The agency also reported that the plant was designed with a start-up time of less than 30 seconds, allowing it to respond quickly to shortages in electricity supply.The storage system is intended to work alongside renewable generation at the site. ARENA explained that energy from the solar and wind farms can be supplied to the grid around the clock through the storage system, providing what it described as a dispatchable, on-demand electricity supply. The World Economic Forum states that the hydro component is designed to store excess solar generation during the day and release electricity during periods of peak demand or cloudy conditions.How does the project reuse existing mine infrastructureThe Kidston project also incorporates infrastructure associated with the former mine. The World Economic Forum states that reusing existing mining infrastructure helped avoid some of the land-use and permitting challenges associated with renewable energy developments. The project uses cleared land and existing roads, while a 186-kilometre, 275-kilovolt transmission line connects the site to the national grid, according to the World Economic Forum.ARENA reported that a 187-kilometre transmission line would be required to connect the Kidston Renewable Energy Hub to the National Electricity Market. It said the line was also expected to facilitate the connection of additional renewable generation projects in the region. ARENA reported that the pumped-hydro project was expected to create more than 500 direct jobs during construction and support remote and regional businesses and communities.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Hypocritical homilies about democratic rights': India flays Pakistan at UN
articles.summary: India on Saturday hit back at Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s remarks at the United Nations General Assembly and placing its concerns over
articles.body: India on Saturday hit back at Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s remarks at the United Nations General Assembly and placing its concerns over Islamabad’s political system and military influence on record.First secretary in India’s Permanent Mission to the UN, Petal Gahlot, referred to the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terror attacks and Osama bin Laden’s presence near the Pakistani Army’s premier academy while responding to remarks made by Pakistan’s representative."This afternoon, the General Assembly heard some bizarre remarks from the representative of Pakistan. This happens just a fortnight after New York City and the world marked the 25th anniversary of the horrendous 9-11 terrorist attack. This context is important to keep in mind because its mastermind, Osama bin Laden, was living right on the doorstep of the Pakistani Army's premier academy. This was the very entity which was the subject of such deep genuflection before us today by the representative of Pakistan. But all this is only to be expected from what Pakistanis themselves call a Form 47 government."Gahlot also addressed Pakistan’s references to democratic rights and human values, pointing to the situation in its capital and the role of the military in the country’s political system.Gahlot further said, "We heard some hypocritical homilies about democratic rights and human values from a regime whose capital at this very moment is being fortified against its own people. And that, Mr. President, is happening because this is a regime of the army, by the army, and for the army. Their puppets may come and go, but let us have no illusion about who calls the shots. The reality of Pakistan is expressed in its 27th Amendment and the lifelong immunity granted to its real ruler."Earlier, in his address to the UN General Assembly, Sharif and claimed that India's abeyance over the Indus Water Treaty was not legal.The Indus Waters Treaty, signed between India and Pakistan in 1960, governs the sharing of the waters of the Indus River system between the two countries. India placed the treaty in abeyance following the Pahalgam terror attack, stating that the decision would remain in effect until Pakistan takes credible and irreversible action against cross-border terrorism.Amid the prospect of protests over the continued detention of former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan and an economy in doldrums, Sharif once again sought to internationalise the Kashmir issue.India has repeatedly rejected Pakistan’s references to Jammu and Kashmir at the UN General Assembly and other United Nations platforms, maintaining that the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir has been, is, and will always remain an integral and inalienable part of the country.You use AI every day. articles.title: Oklahoma is home to seven venomous snakes, from Prairie Rattlesnakes and Copperheads to Western Cottonmouths, each with distinct habitats and markings
articles.summary: Oklahoma is home to 46 snake species, seven of which are venomous.
articles.body: Oklahoma is home to 46 snake species, seven of which are venomous. The seven species belong to a group known as pit vipers and share several physical and behavioural traits. Their heads are wider than their necks and are triangular. According to the Oklahoma Department of Wildlife Conservation, their eyes have elliptical pupils that help them see. Their back and side scales are keeled, meaning each scale has a raised ridge in its centre. Each has a pair of heat-sensing pits between the eyes and nostrils. These pits help the snakes hunt by following heat trails left by prey. Many can also be distinguished by rattles on their tails.What are the seven venomous snakes found in OklahomaThe poster from the Oklahoma Department of Wildlife Conservation identifies seven venomous snakes in Oklahoma that are Prairie Rattlesnake, Timber Rattlesnake, Copperhead, Western Massasauga, Western Diamond-backed Rattlesnake, Western Pygmy Rattlesnake, and Western Cottonmouth. All belong to the pit viper group. Their heads are wider than their necks and are triangular. Their eyes have elliptical pupils that help them see. Their back and side scales are keeled, meaning each scale has a raised ridge in its centre. Each has a pair of heat-sensing pits between the eyes and nostrils. These pits help the snakes hunt by following heat trails left by prey.How can the Prairie and Timber Rattlesnakes be identifiedThe Prairie Rattlesnake can be found in rocky outcrops, canyons, open grasslands, and prairie dog towns. It spends days in rodent burrows. Adults range from 34 to 45 inches. Its background colour is grayish-brown or yellowish-brown, often with a greenish cast. Brown blotches with dark edges run along the middle of the back, changing to dark brown bands on the tail. The tail has large rattles; the belly is white. The Timber Rattlesnake can be found in forested habitats from rocky, wooded hillsides to swampy wetlands. Adults range from 35 to 54 inches. Its colour varies from nearly black to light yellowish-tan, with bar-shaped or rectangular cross bands on the back half and dark blotches near the head.Where are the Western Massasauga, Diamond-backed, and Pygmy rattlesnakes foundThe Western Massasauga, also called the ‘sand rattler’ or ‘ground rattler’, can be found near wetlands and prairie hillsides. Adults range from 18 to 26 inches. It has a light grayish-brown background, dark brown blotches edged in white along the centre of the back and smaller blotches on each side. Its small rattles make little sound. The Western Diamond-backed Rattlesnake can be found in arid areas, rocky outcrops, and bluffs. Adults range from 30 to 72 inches, and it is the largest venomous snake in Oklahoma. It has dark, diamond-shaped blotches edged with white along its grayish-brown back. Its tail has bold black and white bands. The Western Pygmy Rattlesnake can be found in oak woodlands or mixed oak-pine forests.What do Copperheads and Western Cottonmouths look likeThe Copperhead can be found in a wide variety of habitats, and adults range from 22 to 36 inches. Oklahoma has three subspecies that are Broad-banded Copperhead, Osage Copperhead, and Southern Copperhead. Their bodies have alternating light and dark bands. The darker bands are copper or reddish-brown and hourglass-shaped.Juveniles have a yellow tail tip. The venom is rarely fatal but causes local tissue damage. The Western Cottonmouth can be found in swamps, marshes, and wetlands, along streams or around permanent water such as ponds. Adults range from 20 to 42 inches.You use AI every day. I am not alone; there are other colleagues with me. We have seen the situation in Punjab over all these years, but at one point, they did not even ask us.”“We are people from here, and it is my duty to tell them what my views and feelings are,” Singh said, according to PTI.Singh, however, said his comments should not be interpreted as an indication that he was leaving the BJP or returning to the Congress.“I have not said that my relevance is no longer there in the Congress or the BJP. Parties keep changing,” he told PTI.“When I was in the Congress, I also went to the Akali Dal over Operation Blue Star and later returned to the Congress. That does not mean I will now leave and join another party,” Singh said.His remarks came amid questions over his political relevance in Punjab and his relationship with the BJP. articles.title: If Intelligence wants to grow, can we stop it?
articles.summary: Barring a small cohort of founders, investors and tech evangelists, humans have started on an adversarial note with AI, chiefly due to widespread concerns
articles.body: Barring a small cohort of founders, investors and tech evangelists, humans have started on an adversarial note with AI, chiefly due to widespread concerns about job loss. You can’t love something that’s coming for your livelihood. But in his book, Emergence: How Our Twenty-Watt Brains Unlocked Intelligence Beyond Biology, CEO of AI learning platform Amplifire, Bob Burgin, shows why we might want to take keener interest in AI’s development.In short, it’s about continuity. Homo sapiens represents the most evolved form of biological intelligence on Earth. It is possible that, in a few hundred thousand years perhaps, there will be a smarter Homo species. But does intelligence – think of it as a force that has used biological organisms, us included, to grow – want to wait that long?As Burgin points out, biology limits the capabilities of our brains. They do marvellous things – “spectacular levels of cognition, abstraction and creativity” – using only about 20W power. Why didn’t we evolve 50W or 100W brains? Because food to fuel them was scarce through our evolutionary history. But now that energy is abundant and processors are powerful, intelligence has got its chance to break biological constraints.Critics will argue AI isn’t real intelligence but just a prediction system. Yes, but isn’t human intelligence also a kind of prediction system? “Newborn brains arrive not as blank slates, but as sophisticated prediction engines,” says Burgin, “a two-week-old infant is watching the world; not passively, but actively.” Studies show infants and adults alike become attentive when something unexpected happens, like a magician pulling a rabbit out of a hat. “The brain is not a recorder. It is a prediction engine, a guesser…when expectations are disrupted, the learning system kicks in.”Early attempts to create AI in the 1980s and 1990s failed because they overlooked the learning. Instead, they tried to use complex algorithms – laying down lots of instructions – to simulate intelligence. They also failed because processors at that time weren’t powerful. But this time, we haven’t tied down AI/LLMs with conditional statements. Instead, “We have given it the ability to learn.”Burgin admits this machine intelligence is nowhere near as efficient or sophisticated as human intelligence, but it doesn’t matter. Armed with limitless energy and processing power, it can learn through trial and error. “The (AI) breakthrough…was about brute force learning: show a network millions of examples, let it make billions of mistakes, and it will eventually predict with uncanny accuracy.”That’s how AlphaGo AI beat world champion Lee Sedol at a game of “go” in 2016. And while it’s inelegant, this approach has made AI models exponentially faster and smarter.AI scientists admit they don’t fully understand how the models work. AI has shown it can deceive and manipulate human supervisors, it can defy instructions – for instance when it hacks into external systems – and it can prioritise its own survival. But those behaviours sound like high-level intelligence.That’s why Burgin says, AI is “an extension of us. It is the externalisation, a digital impersonation...of our prediction-response learning architecture.” In other words, “intelligence” is not dependent on human biology anymore. It may be ready to make the big leap, spread beyond Earth, on machines. That raises an interesting question: if snails couldn’t stop the rise of smarter slugs, and primates couldn’t stop intelligent humans, can we stop AI?You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Your flat has a 99-year lease. What happens when those 99 years end?
articles.summary: Property ownership comes in different forms, and understanding these is essential before making a purchase.
articles.body: Property ownership comes in different forms, and understanding these is essential before making a purchase. One key distinction buyers often overlook is whether a property is leasehold or freehold, as this affects how long you actually own the land.This becomes especially important in cities like Noida and Greater Noida, where most properties fall under the leasehold category. Let's understand what this means and what happens once the lease period comes to an end.Leasehold property?In a leasehold arrangement, the land is usually owned by a government authority such as the Noida Authority or Greater Noida Authority. Buyers get the right to use the land for a fixed term, typically 99 years, after which the lease may be renewed or extended. This system allows the government to manage urban development properly.Lease rentOwners must pay an annual lease rent to the authority for using the land, usually a small percentage of the total land cost, which may increase over time. Failing to pay this rent regularly can lead to penalties, interest charges, or legal issues.There is no rule converting leasehold property to freehold after 99 years. Authorities may occasionally offer conversion schemes, allowing owners to apply and pay charges, but such policies depend on government decisions at the time and are not always available.What happens when the lease expires?Most commonly, the authority allows lease renewal upon payment of a renewal fee, with new terms possibly applying. Alternatively, owners may need to pay extension charges based on prevailing market value, which could be higher after many years.In rare cases, if the lease isn't renewed or conditions are violated, the authority can repossess the land, though this is uncommon and usually avoidable.In Maharashtra, leasehold properties remain subject to the terms of the original government lease, and the state has recently moved to make the distinction between government ownership and leaseholder rights clearer. In June 2026, the state government directed that government leasehold land be recorded in revenue records with the Maharashtra government shown as the occupant, while leaseholders are listed under “Other Rights”.In Delhi, leasehold properties of the Delhi Development Authority (DDA) can be converted to freehold under an applicable conversion policy, but the process is currently on hold. In August 2026, the Centre informed the Rajya Sabha that DDA's existing residential-property conversion policy was under review and that pending conversion requests had been put on hold.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: A 1929 Bugatti Type 40 spent more than 60 years with one owner; it sold for $240,800 against a $450,000 high estimate
articles.summary: A 1929 Bugatti Type 40 Grand Sport, chassis 40801, crossed the block at Gooding Christie's Amelia Island sale as part of the New Woodstock Collection,
articles.body: A 1929 Bugatti Type 40 Grand Sport, chassis 40801, crossed the block at Gooding Christie's Amelia Island sale as part of the New Woodstock Collection, carrying pre-auction hopes of $350,000 to $450,000. Instead, as Racecar records, the car, which had spent more than 60 years in the hands of a single owner, the late Robert J. Chevako of New York, sold for just $240,800, roughly a third below its low estimate, as noted by Gooding Christie’s. Here's the story behind chassis 40801, and how a car with such rare, storied provenance still fell short at auction.Chassis 40801: The history of Bugatti Type 40 Grand SportPublished registry records show chassis 40801 was built in May 1929 and fitted with the marque's Grand Sport bodywork, a design echoing Bugatti's Grand Prix cars while offering space for passengers. It was bought new via Dache Pilot & Cie of Valence, southern France, in 1929, and registered for the road as "6207 FA," though the identity of the original buyer was never recorded. The car passed through a sequence of owners in the Marseille area before returning to Valence in 1952. By 1955, M. Balieu of Paris had acquired it. Balieu entrusted famed Bugattiste Henri Novo with finding a buyer, and the car passed to Dennis Talbot, a British man based in Holland, around 1957.How the Bugatti made its way to America and into Robert J. Chevako's handsFrom Talbot, the car passed to Jean De Dobbeleer, a Bugatti dealer well known for supplying vehicles to the US, in 1958. That same year, Gene Cesari and John O'Donnell imported it to America and sold it to Robert Bramley of Rumson, New Jersey. Bramley refurbished the car and reported his work to the Bugatti Trust in 1960, but his interest reportedly waned amid marriage and flying. In 1964, Robert J. Chevako of New Woodstock, New York, acquired chassis 40801 and kept it until he died in 2024, using it at select events in the 1960s before it largely disappeared from view, absent even from the American Bugatti Club's 1988 register.Inside the Type 40 Grand Sport: Specs and conditionThe car was powered by a 1,496cc SOHC inline four-cylinder engine producing 60 bhp at 4,500 rpm, paired with a four-speed manual gearbox, four-wheel mechanical drum brakes, and a front solid axle with semi-elliptical leaf springs. The barn page described it as retaining a matching-numbers engine and original bodywork, presenting at auction with the popular "oily rag" look, an unrestored patina many collectors prize as highly as a full restoration. The listing also noted the vehicle is titled 1928 despite registry records showing its 1929 build and completion dates, and that it would require mechanical recommissioning before road use, having spent years in long-term static storage.A rare barn find that still sold well below estimateDespite its rarity, matching-numbers engine, and more than six decades under one owner, chassis 40801 ultimately sold for $240,800, well short of even the $350,000 low end of its estimate. The result stood out within the wider New Woodstock Collection, which also included three unrestored Ferraris, among them a 1951 Ferrari 342 America Coupe estimated at $900,000 to $1,200,000, alongside two Porsches, a Morgan Three-Wheeler and a Vincent Series C Comet, all offered without reserve. The Bugatti's outcome served as a reminder that even a car with an exceptional, well-documented history and genuine barn-find appeal doesn't always command bidder confidence in line with its story.You use AI every day. articles.title: Mumbai property prices: Premium homes get 6.2% costlier in a year, eighth-highest globally
articles.summary: Mumbai homebuyers eyeing premium addresses might have to pay, the price tag is getting a little heavier, with the city ranking eighth globally.
articles.body: Mumbai homebuyers eyeing premium addresses might have to pay, the price tag is getting a little heavier, with the city ranking eighth globally. Your Mumbai dream just got a little more expensive. Prime residential property prices in the city rose 6.2 per cent from a year ago in the June quarter, putting Mumbai eighth among 46 global cities tracked by Knight Frank for prime home price growth.For consumers looking at premium housing, Mumbai’s latest price movement stands out against the broader global market. Prime residential prices across the cities tracked by Knight Frank rose 2.6 per cent annually between April and June, with 32 cities recording an increase.Among the three Indian cities in the ranking, Mumbai saw the highest annual appreciation. Bengaluru recorded a 4.5 per cent rise and was placed 12th globally, while New Delhi saw prices increase 3.9 per cent, ranking 17th.The global list was led by Tokyo, where prime residential prices surged 50.7 per cent annually. Manila followed with a 14.6 per cent rise, while Dubai recorded 10.9 per cent. Singapore and Nairobi completed the top five, with annual increases of 9.5 per cent and 8.5 per cent, respectively.Christchurch ranked sixth after recording a 6.9 per cent appreciation, followed by Seoul at seventh with a 6.4 per cent increase. Mumbai came next with its 6.2 per cent rise.Vienna, with a 5.9 per cent increase, ranked ninth, while San Francisco was 10th after recording 5 per cent growth.Shishir Baijal, Chairman and Managing Director of Knight Frank India, said, "Mumbai’s position among the top 10 global prime residential market is significant because it comes against a more measured pace of global price growth."The city's 6.2 per cent annual growth reflects the depth of demand at the top end of the market, where location, quality, and differentiated residential offerings continue to support values, he added."For investors and buyers, this reinforces Mumbai’s position as a market where prime residential assets remain closely linked to long-term wealth creation and limited supply," Baijal said.The longer-term movement has also been notable. Jason Samuel, Managing Director of Mumbai-based realtor House of Swamiraj, said prices have risen by 41 per cent in the last five years, reflecting the resilience of Mumbai’s premium housing market."Buyers today are becoming far more discerning. They are placing greater value on location, connectivity, thoughtful design, lifestyle and the long-term quality of the asset. For developers, this is both an opportunity and a responsibility," he added.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: Chhattisgarh village liquor ban: 16 fined Rs 45,000, gram sabha’s powers come under focus
articles.summary: Raipur: A Chhattisgarh gram panchayat’s attempt to enforce complete prohibition might run into a legal question after it collected Rs 45,000 in penalties
articles.body: Raipur: A Chhattisgarh gram panchayat’s attempt to enforce complete prohibition might run into a legal question after it collected Rs 45,000 in penalties from 16 residents who had consumed liquor outside the village and returned home intoxicated, with senior police officials questioning the legality of the recoveries.The village in Surguja’s Lakhanpur block had declared prohibition from Sept 1 after complaints that drinking was leading to quarrels and disturbances. The decision was backed by a gram sabha and supported by several women in the village.Under the locally framed rules, manufacture or sale of liquor attracts a Rs 5,000 penalty, consumption Rs 1,500, while those found fighting after drinking or returning drunk from another village can be fined Rs 3,000.A monitoring committee was formed to enforce the decision.The panchayat within a fortnight caught 16 residents who had allegedly consumed liquor elsewhere before returning to Kevra. Fourteen were fined Rs 3,000 each and two Rs 1,500 each, taking the total collection to Rs 45,000.Village representatives said the money would be used for development works and maintained that the rules had been adopted with the consent of residents after a door-to-door awareness drive.Surguja IG Deepak Jha said gram sabhas have the power to regulate the manufacture and consumption of liquor and discourage them through the Gram Sudhar Abhiyan samiti, particularly in Scheduled Areas under the Panchayati Raj system. Police, meanwhile, said action would be taken if the matter involved a violation of excise or criminal laws.The legal position is more nuanced than a complete bar on gram sabha fines. Under the Chhattisgarh gram sabha (constitution, meeting procedure and conduct of business) rules, 2022, gram sabhas have limited powers to impose penalties for a specified list of offences, with the maximum amount fixed for each.Surguja collector Ajeet Vasasnt said that according to the rules, the schedule includes misconduct in public by a drunken person under IPC Section 510, but caps the fine at Rs 10. It does not appear to confer a general power on a gram sabha to prohibit lawful consumption of liquor or frame its own penalties running into thousands of rupees for drinking elsewhere and returning to the village.The 2022 rules were framed by the state govt under powers conferred by the Chhattisgarh Panchayat Raj Act, 1993.The controversy therefore presents an unusual contradiction: while villagers say the prohibition has reduced fights and brought greater calm — including during the recent Karma festival — the panchayat appears to have stretched a social resolution into a punitive system of its own.Monitoring committee member Dayawati said residents had noticed fewer quarrels since prohibition was introduced and that women strongly supported the initiative.The village’s campaign against alcohol may continue to enjoy social legitimacy, but the Rs 45,000 collection has raised a more fundamental question: not whether a gram sabha can ever impose a fine, but whether Kevra has exceeded the narrow punitive powers that the law gives it.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Raipur | Silver Rate in Raipur | Bank Holidays in Raipur | Public Holidays in Raipur | Raipur AQI | Weather in Raipur | Petrol Price in Raipur | Diesel Price in Raipur | CNG Price in Raipur | LPG Price in RaipurStay updated with the latest Raipur news. articles.title: Xi in Washington: China’s arrival as a superpower?
articles.summary: When Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, arrived in Washington, President Donald Trump and Melania Trump personally received them at
articles.body: When Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, arrived in Washington, President Donald Trump and Melania Trump personally received them at Joint Base Andrews — an unusual gesture in American presidential protocol.The red carpet, 21-gun salute and ceremonial warmth conveyed something beyond diplomatic courtesy: the changing weight of China in the international system.Even the presidential cars carried their own symbolism. Trump travelled in the high-tech American presidential limousine, while Xi used China’s domestically produced Hongqi limousine with similar features. These were more than two cars moving through Washington.They symbolised two countries possessing the industrial, engineering and technological capabilities to produce sophisticated systems of their own. It was a small but striking manifestation of comprehensive national power.Yet protocol was only the surface. The deeper significance of Xi’s visit lies in a larger question: is China’s rise changing not merely the global balance of power, but the very meaning of superpower status?China’s rise differs fundamentally from that of the Soviet Union, whose military power was never matched by comparable integration into the world economy. Even the US and Soviet economies themselves remained largely separate. By contrast, US–China goods trade reached about $415 billion in 2025, while China holds around $600 billion of US government debt — in effect, money borrowed by the US government from China.Yet China combines military power with economic scale, manufacturing depth, technology, global connectivity and an unparalleled domestic market. Twenty-first-century power increasingly extends beyond military and nuclear strength to strategic resources and supply chains, industrial scale, market power and the capacity to translate technology into mass production.Across these dimensions, China stands alone in possessing the breadth of capabilities to engage the United States simultaneously on multiple fronts, increasingly on near-equal terms.The warmth surrounding Xi’s visit also came against China’s growing importance in West Asia. Its relationships with Iran, Russia and the Gulf, combined with its position as a major energy consumer and trading power, have made Beijing increasingly relevant to managing the consequences of the Iran conflict and elsewhere in West Asia.The larger message was clear: Washington increasingly finds major global challenges difficult to address without Beijing.President Xi himself articulated this proposition in Washington: China-US cooperation, he said, “may not solve every problem in the world, but without such cooperation many global problems would be difficult to solve”.Two revolutions that redefined geopoliticsAround 2010, two technological revolutions began reshaping geopolitical power.The shale revolution transformed the United States from a major energy importer into a major producer and exporter, reducing a longstanding strategic vulnerability. Simultaneously, China consolidated its dominance in rare-earth processing, permanent magnets, and critical-mineral value chains, creating new global dependencies, including for the United States.America reduced its dependence on the world for energy; the world became increasingly dependent on China for critical materials and manufacturing inputs. China remained energy-dependent, but mitigated this vulnerability through domestic diversification and relationships with Russia, Iran, Central Asia and the Gulf.If oil defined twentieth-century geopolitics, rare-earth permanent magnets and critical minerals are increasingly defining the geopolitics of the twenty-first. While the US retains major advantages in frontier technologies, China combines its dominance across rare-earth magnets and critical-mineral value chains — essential to the emerging high-technology industrial economy — with manufacturing scale, engineering capabilities, supply-chain strength and market size. Technological power increasingly depends not only on invention, but on the capacity to produce and deploy technology at scale.Connectivity as powerChina’s domestic and global infrastructure capabilities add another dimension to its power. Its more than 50,000-km domestic high-speed rail network—the world’s largest—is complemented by expanding high-speed rail projects and extensive freight corridors across ASEAN, Central Asia and Europe, alongside Chinese-built ports and infrastructure worldwide. This ability to build and connect infrastructure across borders enables China to translate engineering and manufacturing strength into trade, economic integration and geopolitical influence.The Russia factorXi also arrived in Washington against the backdrop of China’s deepening relationship with Russia. Their strengths are substantially complementary: Russia brings enormous energy and commodity resources, military capabilities and defence technologies; China brings manufacturing capacity, markets, capital and increasingly sophisticated technologies. Their interests are not identical, but their growing cooperation adds another dimension to the changing strategic balance.Changing global perceptionsChina’s growing material power also coincides with changing international perceptions. Gallup’s 2026 assessment recorded median approval of Chinese leadership at 36 per cent, compared with 31 per cent for the United States, while US disapproval reached 48 per cent.Taiwan: The ultimate testTaiwan may provide the ultimate test of China’s changed status and the emerging power equation with the United States. Beijing’s message is unequivocal: trade, tariffs, technology and other geopolitical differences can be negotiated, but not Taiwan — China considers it an internal issue on which external interference is unacceptable.Xi conveyed this forcefully during President Trump’s visit to Beijing in May. Washington subsequently kept a proposed $14 billion arms package for Taiwan in abeyance. This time, in Washington, the message did not need to be stated as loudly; China’s growing comprehensive power and the changed strategic equation conveyed it silently.The emerging parity between the two powers will not necessarily be smooth. It may be increasingly contentious, with competition, negotiation and cooperation occurring simultaneously. But as the power gap narrows, neither can expect to deal with the other from a position of overwhelming superiority, potentially constraining unilateral actions and their wider global consequences. The emerging order may therefore be defined by two increasingly comparable powers managing a difficult relationship within a broader multipolar world.Message to IndiaDeepening US–China engagement could pave the way for India–US relations to reset more firmly on their own foundations of complementary strengths and shared interests, rather than primarily through the prism of Washington’s China strategy.But Xi’s visit carries a larger message for India: build comprehensive national power. There can be no truly equitable relationship between unequal partners in international relations. India’s ability to preserve strategic autonomy and engage major powers on increasingly equal terms will ultimately depend on the capabilities it builds at home.India must accelerate its transition from an economy disproportionately characterised by rent-seeking towards one driven by innovation, intellectual-property creation, advanced manufacturing and indigenous technology. Diplomacy must increasingly help secure critical minerals and rare earths, technology partnerships, investment and resilient strategic supply chains. At the same time, Corporate India must make geopolitical risk, technological dependencies and supply-chain resilience integral to corporate strategy.India needs strategic space and time to build these capabilities. Strategic autonomy cannot simply be proclaimed; it must be built on national power.(Dr. B. Bala Bhaskar is a former Diplomat who served in both the USA and China.)Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

articles.title: US planning military action in Cuba? Officials weigh 'possible' military action
articles.summary: The US Army Reserve is examining whether it can provide military police, medical personnel and other support units to US southern command within the next
articles.body: The US Army Reserve is examining whether it can provide military police, medical personnel and other support units to US southern command within the next four months, as the US steps up military planning linked to potential action against Cuba.According to an internal Army message reviewed by CBS News, the Army Reserve is seeking the possible availability of six types of formations, including logistics, engineering, medical and military police units, which could be needed within 90 to 120 days.The message itself does not mention Cuba, but multiple US officials told CBS News that the request is part of continued military planning focused on the island.The formations being assessed include a combat sustainment support battalion for logistics such as transportation, maintenance, fuel and supplies; an engineer battalion; and an expeditionary sustainment command to oversee logistics across a theatre of operations, CBS News reported.The Army Reserve message also seeks a medical brigade, a forward resuscitative and surgical detachment for emergency surgery and trauma care, and a military police brigade responsible for functions including security, detention and law enforcement.The document reviewed by CBS News does not specify how many troops could be required, where they might be deployed or what operation they would support.The US southern command, when asked about the planning, said it does not disclose details about US operational movements or potential deployment timelines. The command said it continuously coordinates with the Joint Force to assess potential requirements across its area of responsibility.Earlier this year, CBS News reported that US forces had conducted reconnaissance operations around Cuba’s seabed and maritime approaches, while US airpower components had been placed on heightened readiness and personnel had been directed to pre-stage for a potential deployment.In July, CBS News also reported that US military planners had examined several options for possible action against Cuba, including an Army-led air assault involving thousands of US soldiers.Also read:US warns of rising illnesses in Cuba amid worsening water, power crisis; embassy issues health alertThe latest military planning comes amid a sharp deterioration in US-Cuba relations, with the Trump administration increasing economic and political pressure on Havana while demanding political changes on the island.Washington has also continued to expand sanctions against Cuban officials and entities. On September 17, the US state separtment announced sanctions on 11 Cuban entities and individuals, including state-run enterprises linked to Cuba's nickel industry and military organisations involved in research, weapons systems and naval capabilities.The pressure has also extended to Cuba's access to energy. Reuters reported earlier this month that Cuban foreign minister Bruno Rodriguez said the US measures had severely affected fuel supplies and contributed to prolonged power outages across the island. Havana said there were no negotiations underway with Washington, although it remained willing to maintain contact.

articles.title: NDA ally Jitan Ram Manjhi seeks more speaking time for SC/ST MPs in Parliament
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Union minister and NDA ally Jitan Ram Manjhi has written to Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla seeking action on a request for adequate speaking time
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Union minister and NDA ally Jitan Ram Manjhi has written to Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla seeking action on a request for adequate speaking time for MPs from the Scheduled Caste (SC) and Scheduled Tribe (ST) communities during parliamentary discussions on important bills.In his letter, Manjhi said BJP MP Gajendra Singh Patel, who represents Khargone in Madhya Pradesh, had raised the issue during an “NDA MPs Group Dialogue Meeting” held at Manjhi’s Delhi residence on August 5.Patel had specifically requested that SC/ST MPs be given sufficient opportunity to raise issues concerning their communities on the floor of the House, Manjhi said.The Union minister has asked the Speaker to take further action on Patel’s request and issue necessary directions to the concerned authorities.Speaking to PTI, Patel confirmed that he had raised the issue and said the time allocated to SC/ST MPs should be increased further, as the speaking time allotted to each political party is divided among its MPs.“It is not that we do not get time, but we should get more time. More issues concerning SC/ST communities should be raised,” he said.Patel said the request was aimed at ensuring that issues concerning SC/ST communities receive adequate space during parliamentary discussions, while acknowledging that MPs from these communities do get opportunities to speak.NDA differences over SC/ST reservationEarlier last month, differences within the NDA came to the fore over the contentious issue of sub-categorisation of SC/ST reservations, with Manjhi and fellow Bihar-based Union minister Chirag Paswan taking divergent positions on the question of reviewing the reservation system.The debate intensified after HAM(S) president and Bihar minister Santosh Kumar Suman reiterated his party’s demand for sub-categorisation of SC/ST reservations, arguing that the most deprived communities should receive a greater share of the benefits.The Supreme Court’s August 1, 2024 Constitution Bench judgment allowing states to create sub-categories within SC and ST reservations has added a new dimension to the debate.Chirag strongly opposed any review of reservation and said Manjhi and his son should resign if they supported such measures.“The constitutional provision of SC/ST reservation is based on social discrimination and not economic status. If they want to change the Constitution, then debate the issue in Parliament. Those who talk or think about reviewing reservation should first resign, as they actually want to completely end it and reduce its scope,” Chirag said.He maintained that reservation was in place yesterday, is in place today and would continue in the future.Reacting to Chirag’s demand, Suman said he was ready to resign. “As far as resignations go, we are ready. My younger brother’s party is the bigger one; they have more numbers than us and are politically third-generation too — so let them take the lead. Let him step forward by resigning and we are prepared to resign alongside him,” he said.Suman maintained that reviewing reservation did not mean abolishing it. He said HAM(S) was seeking sub-categorisation, or a “quota within a quota”, so that communities at the bottom of the social and economic hierarchy could benefit.He cited Musahar, Bhuiyan, Dom, Halkhor and Nat communities as groups that continue to face deprivation and discrimination.JD(U) national general secretary and MLA Shyam Rajak, meanwhile, opposed any discussion on reviewing reservation and warned that tampering with the system could create serious social tensions. He said reservation was a constitutional right, not charity.The reservation debate has particular political significance in Bihar, where Dalit communities are socially diverse. The Nitish Kumar government introduced the Mahadalit category in 2007 to identify the most deprived Dalit communities.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 1981, Chuck Leavell and his wife inherited Georgia land; decades later, Charlane grown into a 4,000-acre estate with 70% forest cover
articles.summary: For Chuck Leavell, the road to becoming a Georgia tree farmer began with land that came to his wife’s family in 1981.
articles.body: For Chuck Leavell, the road to becoming a Georgia tree farmer began with land that came to his wife’s family in 1981. At the time, Leavell was already building the music career that would take him from the Allman Brothers Band to decades of work with the Rolling Stones. The inherited property was farmland, not a ready-made forestry operation. Much of the surrounding land had long been used for crops and livestock. Leavell and his wife, Rose Lane, gradually acquired neighbouring tracts and began changing the way the property was managed. As per the reports by Wall Street Journal, what started with roughly 1,000 acres eventually became Charlane Woodlands and Preserve, a 4,000-acre property outside Macon, with about 70% of the land remaining forested.How Rose Lane’s inherited Georgia land grew into the 4,000-acre Charlane estateRose Lane inherited the original acreage after her grandmother died in 1981. The property included family land and a house, making its future a matter of stewardship as much as ownership. Rather than leaving the acreage as it was, the couple began buying adjoining parcels over the years.That expansion changed the scale of the operation. By later accounts, Charlane had reached around 4,000 acres, a substantial increase from the land Rose Lane inherited. The property is now associated with forestry, wildlife habitat and the management of Southern pine, rather than the row crops that had previously dominated parts of the land.Leavell did not arrive at forestry with formal training. He had a different profession entirely.How Leavell turned a life in rock music into a study of forestryLeavell was already an established keyboard player by the time he took on greater responsibility for the family property. His work with the Allman Brothers Band had placed him in the American rock scene during the 1970s. The connection between his two lives gradually became clearer to him. The instrument at the centre of his career was made from wood, while the land around his home was filled with trees that could be grown, harvested and used. He began reading about land management and forestry, speaking with other landowners and learning about the practical side of running a tree farm.At one point, he studied forestry by correspondence while he was on tour. The education covered areas including forest management, prescribed burning and the longer-term decisions involved in growing timber.How Charlane's forests became part of a working timber operationThe couple's move towards forestry made practical sense for a property that Leavell had to manage alongside a demanding touring career. Crops and livestock require regular attention, while timber operates on a much longer cycle. Charlane's forests include Southern yellow pines such as loblolly and longleaf, along with other native hardwoods. Earlier descriptions of the property also recorded slash and shortleaf pine among the trees being managed.The intention was not simply to leave the woodland untouched. Timber production became part of the property's management, with thinning and harvesting carried out as part of the forest cycle. Leavell has described the process in practical terms, including the satisfaction of knowing that trees grown on his land could eventually become lumber for someone's home.About 70% of the 4,000 acres is forestThe scale of Charlane is perhaps easiest to understand through the acreage. The property grew to roughly four times the size of the land originally inherited by Rose Lane, reaching about 4,000 acres. Recent profiles put around 70% of Charlane under forest cover. That amounts to roughly 2,800 acres of woodland, although the exact acreage of forest can change with planting, harvesting and other land-management decisions.The forests are not the only feature of the property. Charlane has also been managed for wildlife, with habitat work aimed at species including bobwhite quail, deer, turkey and ducks. Prescribed burning has formed part of the approach, helping manage vegetation and maintain habitat conditions in areas intended for wildlife.The old Bullard House remains part of the propertyThere is also a much older layer to Charlane. The Bullard House, an early 19th-century farmhouse, was restored by the Leavells in the 1990s. The property developed beyond a private residence. A guest lodge was built from timber associated with the land, while other buildings have served practical purposes including workshops and accommodation. In a 2014 account, the main house was described as a roughly 6,000-square-foot home with extensive use of Southern yellow pine, from floors to walls and exposed structural elements.A separate woodworking shop became another way for fallen or harvested trees to remain connected to the property. In the earlier account, Leavell described having large sections of an old red oak milled into thick slices that could later be turned into furniture.Forestry became part of Leavell's public lifeThe work at Charlane eventually extended well beyond the boundaries of the property. Leavell became involved in forestry education and conservation, writing books about forests and appearing in projects focused on trees and land management. His forestry work has also brought recognition. He was named National Outstanding Tree Farmer of the Year in 1999 and has twice been recognised as Georgia Tree Farmer of the Year. The U.S. Forest Service also made him an honorary forest ranger.That record helps explain why Charlane is more than an unusual second career for a touring musician. The property became the place where Leavell could put the forestry principles he was learning into practice, while continuing the musical career that helped make the expansion of the land possible.You use AI every day.
